what: Introduction: Biostatistical Interoperability Between R and SAS
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: regulated clinical biostatistics, collaborative workflows R SAS essential: - Data Exchange: Analysis Data Model (ADaM) Tabulation (SDTM) datasets archived proprietary SAS format (.sas7bdat) SAS transport format (.xpt), yet statistical analysts frequently prototype, explore, visualize using R. - Complex Longitudinal Dynamics: Real clinical trials follow subjects multiple visits, generating counting-process start/stop intervals (tstart, tstop, status). Modeling repeated events, time-dependent covariates, multi-center cluster designs requires rigorous variance estimation. - Clustered Robust Sandwich Variance: counting-process data, multiple observation rows originate patient. Without clustered robust sandwich standard errors (COVS(AGGREGATE)\text{COVS(AGGREGATE)} SAS, cluster(id) / id = id R), model-based standard errors deflated, leading false-positive statistical significance. - Survival Curve Estimation: Estimating adjusted survival probabilities presence time-varying coefficients presents significant challenges: standard baseline estimators (PROC PHREG BASELINE SAS default survfit() R) assume time-invariant relative hazards fail compound time-varying hazard rates correctly. vignette serves operational reference biostatisticians, statistical programmers, validation teams (Dariana, Lu, Temple biostatistics group) covering: Bidirectional Data /O: Reading writing .sas7bdat, .xpt, interchange data preserving column metadata variable labels. Counting Process Data Splitting: Expanding survival follow-discrete risk intervals R (survSplit) SAS (%cpdata). Multi-Center Clinical Benchmark (survival::cgd): Validating clustered robust sandwich standard errors (id = id) multi-center stratified baseline hazards (strata(center)) TempleCBE SAS PROC PHREG. Time-Varying Coefficients & Adjusted Survival: Modeling non-proportional hazards estimating adjusted survival curves using Rossi recidivism cohort via SAS %coxtvc R survfit(..., individual = TRUE). Build validated SAS macro library compile permanent catalogs (sasmacr.sas7bcat). Import macros existing organizational SAS macro libraries (via autocall SASAUTOS= SASMSTORE=). Author, test, register new features local macro library automated batch execution R. Joint Modeling Longitudinal & Survival Processes: Auditing repeated measures via proc_contents(..., subject_id = ...) contrasting multi-paradigm predictive modeling (joint_model()) SAS %JM macro (Rizopoulos 2010, Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos 2018). Master Macro Catalog & Translation Cheat Sheet: Comprehensive reference mapping SAS syntax TempleCBE.

text: SAS Example 85.7, wide dataset Tumor converted start/stop counting-process format using array-driven DATA step: Crucially, SAS programmer added condition (pp[_i_] ^= qq[_i_]) ;: compresses consecutive observation intervals whenever papilloma count change, reducing cohort 428 potential visit intervals 102 compressed intervals.
code: /* SAS Counting-Process Transformation (Example 85.7) */ data Tumor1(keep=ID Time Dead Dose T1 T2 NPap Status);    array pp{*} P1-P14;    array qq{*} P2-P15;    array tt{1:15} _temporary_       (27 34 37 41 43 45 46 47 49 50 51 53 65 67 71);    set Tumor;    T1 = 0; T2 = 0; Status = 0;    if ( Time = tt[1] ) then do;       T2 = tt[1]; NPap = p1; Status = Dead; output;    end;    else do _i_=1 to dim(pp);       if ( tt[_i_] = Time ) then do;          T2 = Time; NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = Dead; output;       end;       else if (tt[_i_] < Time ) then do;          if (pp[_i_] ^= qq[_i_] ) then do;             if qq[_i_] = . then T2 = Time;             else                T2 = tt[_i_];             NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = 0; output;             T1 = T2;          end;       end;    end;    if ( Time >= tt[15] ) then do;       T2 = Time; NPap = P15; Status = Dead; output;    end; run;

text: TempleCBE, pipe-friendly function tidy_tmerge_cox() builds start–stop survival intervals (tstart, tstop, event, event_label) repeated measurement tables, event/censoring tables, baseline covariate tables according standard clinical data registry guidelines:
code: # 1. Load the reference wide tumor dataset (Example 85.7) w <- tumor_wide()  # 2. Reshape wide longitudinal measurements P1..P15 to a tidy measurement frame tt <- c(27, 34, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 65, 67, 71)  measure_list <- list() for (i in seq_len(nrow(w))) {   id_i <- w$ID[i]   p_vals <- as.numeric(w[i, paste0("P", 1:15)])   measure_list[[length(measure_list) + 1]] <- tibble(ID = id_i, time = 0, NPap = p_vals[1])   for (k in 1:15) {     if (!is.na(p_vals[k])) {       measure_list[[length(measure_list) + 1]] <- tibble(ID = id_i, time = tt[k], NPap = p_vals[k])     }   } } measure_df <- bind_rows(measure_list) %>% distinct(ID, time, .keep_all = TRUE)  event_df <- w %>%   select(ID, Time, Dead) %>%   rename(event_time = Time, event_type = Dead)  baseline_df <- w %>%   select(ID, Dose)  # 3. Construct start/stop counting-process intervals via tidy_tmerge_cox tumor_tidy <- tidy_tmerge_cox(   measure_df   = measure_df,   event_df     = event_df,   baseline_df  = baseline_df,   id           = "ID",   measure_time = "time",   event_time   = "event_time",   event_type   = "event_type",   post_event   = "exclude" )  cat("tidy_tmerge_cox created", nrow(tumor_tidy), "clinical visit intervals across", length(unique(tumor_tidy$ID)), "subjects.\n") #> tidy_tmerge_cox created 428 clinical visit intervals across 45 subjects. head(tumor_tidy %>% select(ID, tstart, tstop, event, Dose, NPap), 6) #> # A tibble: 6 × 6 #>      ID tstart tstop event  Dose  NPap #>   <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1     1      0    27     0     1     0 #> 2     1     27    34     0     1     0 #> 3     1     34    37     0     1     5 #> 4     1     37    41     0     1     6 #> 5     1     41    43     0     1     8 #> 6     1     43    45     0     1    10

code: # 1. Define time-varying coefficient interaction on counting process data toy_split$lt_age <- toy_split$age * log(toy_split$time1)  # 2. Fit Cox model with time-varying coefficient fit_tv <- coxph(   Surv(time0, time1, death) ~ female + age + lt_age,   data = toy_split,   ties = "breslow" )  summary(fit_tv)$coefficients #>              coef exp(coef)  se(coef)          z  Pr(>|z|) #> female  1.6422699 5.1668848 2.8381173  0.5786477 0.5628269 #> age    -1.2568579 0.2845467 1.4676221 -0.8563907 0.3917817 #> lt_age  0.1755235 1.1918699 0.5451421  0.3219774 0.7474698  # 3. Build prediction covariate trajectory for a 21-year-old male across all follow-up intervals last_id <- toy_split$id[which.max(toy_split$time1)] target_intervals <- toy_split %>%   filter(id == last_id) %>%   select(time0, time1, death)  pred_trajectory <- data.frame(   age    = 21,   female = 0,   target_intervals ) pred_trajectory$lt_age <- pred_trajectory$age * log(pred_trajectory$time1)  # 4. what: 4.4 Large-Scale Case Study: The Rossi Recidivism Cohort
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: Rossi recidivism study followed 432 released convicts 52 weeks assess whether financial aid (fin) reduced rearrest (arrest = 1). Prior research demonstrated effect financial aid strongest weeks 20 30, age showed decreasing hazard effect time: coefficient fin_mid strongly protective (HR≈0.23,p=0.029\text{HR} \approx 0.23, p = 0.029), demonstrating financial support significantly lowered recidivism risk critical transition period weeks 20 30.
code: # 1. Load data rossi <- rossi_data("csv")[, 1:10] rossi$id <- seq_len(nrow(rossi))  # 2. Split data at unique arrest weeks (generating 19,805 intervals) cut_rossi <- sort(unique(rossi$week[rossi$arrest == 1])) rossi_split <- survSplit(   data  = rossi,   cut   = cut_rossi,   end   = "week",   start = "week0",   event = "arrest" )  cat("Rossi Split Cohort:", nrow(rossi_split), "start/stop intervals.\n") #> Rossi Split Cohort: 18766 start/stop intervals.  # 3. Create time-varying interactions: #    - age_week: age * week (continuous decay) #    - fin_mid:  financial aid effect specifically between weeks 20 and 30 rossi_split$age_week <- rossi_split$age * rossi_split$week rossi_split$fin_mid <- rossi_split$fin * (20 < rossi_split$week & rossi_split$week < 30)  # 4. Fit multivariable time-varying Cox model with clustering on inmate id fit_rossi_tvc <- coxph(   Surv(week0, week, arrest) ~ age + fin + prio + age_week + fin_mid,   data = rossi_split,   id = id,   ties = "breslow" )  # Model summary table tidy_rossi <- broom::tidy(fit_rossi_tvc, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) tidy_rossi %>%   select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value, conf.low, conf.high) #> # A tibble: 5 × 6 #>   term     estimate std.error  p.value conf.low conf.high #>   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 age         1.03    0.0392  0.417      0.956      1.11  #> 2 fin         0.852   0.205   0.436      0.570      1.27  #> 3 prio        1.10    0.0273  0.000337   1.05       1.16  #> 4 age_week    0.996   0.00146 0.00919    0.993      0.999 #> 5 fin_mid     0.234   0.665   0.0288     0.0635     0.860

text: clinical biostatistics, longitudinal biomarkers (CD4 counts HIV tumor marker trajectories oncology) frequently tracked alongside primary survival endpoints. traditional practice, analysts often fit naive time-dependent Cox regression models: hi(t)=h0(t)exp⁡(β1drugi+β2yi(t))h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left(\beta_1 \text{drug}_i + \beta_2 y_i(t)\right) treating observed biomarker yi(t)y_i(t) piecewise step-function via tmerge %cpdata. However, shown Rizopoulos (2010, JSS 35(9)) Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos (2018, JSS 84(12)), naive time-dependent Cox regression suffers two critical flaws: 1. Measurement Error: Endogenous biological markers recorded laboratory noise. Treating error-free covariates biases hazard ratios toward null (attenuation bias). 2. Informative Dropout & Censoring: Patients worse health trajectories drop experience events earlier, creating informative intermittent missingness.

text: targets (rOpenSci, developed Landau) gold standard R function-oriented, computation-driven pipelines. design philosophy centers pure R functions expressions: Computational units: user defines steps via tar_target(name, command) inside central _targets.R script. Dependency discovery: targets inspects Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) user functions automatically detect targets functions feed others. Caching & staleness: Cryptographic hashes functions, expressions, -memory objects detect staleness. function’s code input data changes, downstream targets invalidated. Execution engine: Running tar_make() executes pipeline, stores serialized R objects internal binary cache (_targets/objects/), skips --date targets. supports high-performance computing (HPC) clusters via crew, clustermq, future. targets extraordinarily powerful long-running statistical computations, simulation studies, reproducible research intensive R calculations need cached parallelized.

title: Visualizing Computational Pipeline Dependencies
text: TempleCBE’s compute graph architecture fundamentally file-system artifact-oriented, metadata-rich, non-intrusive. Rather acting heavy execution engine R expressions, serves lightweight, human-interpretable dependency auditor visual communication layer: File-system nodes vs. -memory objects: targets, target usually R variable intermediate data frame stored private cache. TempleCBE, every node tangible file disk (FilePath), inspectable anyone using standard file browsers command-line tools. Zero-rewrite adoption vs. Functional refactoring: Adopting targets demands modularizing analysis scripts pure functions writing central _targets.R configuration. contrast, TempleCBE requires zero source code changes: wrap existing project scripts, templates, raw data files, outputs lightweight metadata manifest without touching single line existing analysis code. Language & format agnosticism: targets can track external files via format = "file" Quarto reports via tar_quarto(), primarily R execution engine. TempleCBE treats files equally: raw .xlsx clinical coordinator, .sas data step, .py preprocessing script, .qmd Quarto document, rendered .pdf .docx deliverable first-class nodes. Domain-aware clinical semantics: targets nodes carry computational statuses (e.g. uptodate, queued, running). TempleCBE nodes carry domain-meaningful metadata: workflow lifecycle milestones (stage), semantic analytical roles (artifact_role: raw data, derived baseline data, imputed data, helper scripts, deliverable reports), modification timestamps (mtime), plain-language descriptions. Decoupled execution vs. Monolithic runner: targets tightly couples dependency analysis execution via tar_make(). TempleCBE decouples staleness planning (get_render_plan()) execution: answers stale topological order must rendered, leaving execution mechanics entirely analyst (e.g. Quarto CLI, RStudio, GNU Make, custom batch scripts). Multi-tier stakeholder communication: targets provides developer diagnostics (tar_visnetwork()), TempleCBE provides rich, publication-ready client-ready deliverables: zoomable HTML widgets rich tooltips, neighborhood ego-subgraphs, custom Sugiyama-layout static PNGs, collapsed stage-level diagrams.

title: Visualizing Computational Pipeline Dependencies
text: production biostatistical pipelines collaborative studies (modeled architecture Wolfson study TempleCBE), best practice encapsulate entire project dependency structure centralized orchestration script named MakeComputeGraph.R. Rather hardcoding ad-hoc graphs interactive sessions, MakeComputeGraph.R provides single source truth entire study lifecycle: Configures study stages & visual identity: Uses pipeline_config() establish human-readable labels color coding every analytical phase. Declares raw & derived assets: Uses FilePath() semantic roles (raw_data, derived_data) analysts know files source registries vs. derived caches. Connects executable reports & vignettes: Uses create_qmd_renderer() link reports explicit data dependencies topological order. TempleCBE ships exact architecture vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R (inst/scripts/MakeComputeGraph.R), orchestrating four analytical vignettes: script run, calling pipeline_summary() resulting pipeline immediately yields structured governance audit across project stages: can also use list_stage_data_artifacts() scan directories catalogue derived data files automatically:
code: library(TempleCBE) library(dplyr)  make_temple_compute_graph <- function() {   # 1. Project Pipeline Configuration   pipeline_config(     study_name = "TempleCBE Biostatistical & Survival Analysis Architecture",     stage_labels = c(       "01_EDA"            = "Exploratory Data Analysis & Quality Audit",       "02_Survival_CV"    = "Penalized Coxnet & Nested Cross-Validation",       "03_Compute_Graph"  = "Pipeline Dependency & Governance Graph",       "04_SAS_Validation" = "SAS PROC PHREG Benchmark Validation"     ),     stage_colors = list(       "01_EDA"            = "#DDEBF7",       "02_Survival_CV"    = "#FCE4D6",       "03_Compute_Graph"  = "#E8DAEF",       "04_SAS_Validation" = "#D4EFDF"     )   )    # 2. Raw Data Inputs   raw_clinical <- FilePath(     name = "raw_patient_registry",     path = "data/raw/patient_registry.csv",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "01_EDA",     artifact_role = "raw_data",     description = "Raw clinical intake data with missing biomarker measurements"   )    sas_benchmark_raw <- FilePath(     name = "tumor_wide_data",     path = "data/raw/Tumor.xlsx",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     artifact_role = "raw_data",     description = "45-animal longitudinal papilloma count study (SAS Example 85.7)"   )    # 3. Stage 01: EDA & Missingness Analysis   cleaned_cohort_rds <- FilePath(     name = "cleaned_cohort_rds",     path = "data/derived/cleaned_cohort.rds",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "01_EDA",     artifact_role = "derived_data",     description = "Audited and normalized clinical cohort"   )    eda_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "01_eda_and_missingness",     path = "vignettes/eda_and_missingness.Rmd",     deps = list(raw_clinical),     file_stage = "01_EDA",     description = "Missingness auditing, outlier fences, and feature normalization"   )   eda_report@output <- c(eda_report@output, list(cleaned_cohort_rds))    # 4. Stage 02: Penalized Coxnet & Nested Cross-Validation   survival_cv_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "02_nested_survival_cv",     path = "vignettes/nested_survival_cv.Rmd",     deps = list(cleaned_cohort_rds),     file_stage = "02_Survival_CV",     description = "Subject-grouped nested cross-validation and elastic-net Cox modeling"   )    # 5. Stage 04: SAS Validation & Time-Dependent Covariates   tumor_cp_rds <- FilePath(     name = "tumor_counting_process_rds",     path = "data/derived/Tumor1.rds",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     artifact_role = "derived_data",     description = "Start/stop counting-process records generated via tidy_tmerge_cox"   )    sas_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "04_sas_survival",     path = "vignettes/sas_survival.Rmd",     deps = list(sas_benchmark_raw),     file_stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     description = "Numerical validation against SAS PROC PHREG and tidy start/stop merging"   )   sas_report@output <- c(sas_report@output, list(tumor_cp_rds))    # 6. Stage 03: Compute Graph & Governance   graph_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "03_compute_graph",     path = "vignettes/compute_graph.Rmd",     deps = list(eda_report, survival_cv_report, sas_report),     file_stage = "03_Compute_Graph",     description = "Dependency graph auditing, staleness detection, and pipeline governance"   )    # Assemble full pipeline   list(     raw_clinical,     sas_benchmark_raw,     eda_report,     cleaned_cohort_rds,     survival_cv_report,     sas_report,     tumor_cp_rds,     graph_report   ) } mcg_path <- if (file.exists("MakeComputeGraph.R")) {   "MakeComputeGraph.R" } else if (file.exists("vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R")) {   "vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R" } else {   system.file("scripts", "MakeComputeGraph.R", package = "TempleCBE") }  if (nzchar(mcg_path) && file.exists(mcg_path)) {   source(mcg_path)   temple_pipe <- make_temple_compute_graph()   pipeline_summary(temple_pipe) } #> ======================================================================== #>                       Computational Pipeline Summary                     #> ======================================================================== #> Total Nodes: 12 | Total Edges: 12 | Stale Nodes: 6 (Needs Re-render) #>  #> Artifact Roles: #>   - deliverable_report        :  4 #>   - derived_data              :  2 #>   - raw_data                  :  2 #>   - report_source             :  4 #>  #> Pipeline Stages Breakdown: #>              stage Reports Data_Files Helpers Total #>             01_EDA       2          2       0     4 #>     02_Survival_CV       2          0       0     2 #>   03_Compute_Graph       2          0       0     2 #>  04_SAS_Validation       2          2       0     4 #> ======================================================================== # Inspect all data files in an imputation output folder stage_artifacts <- list_stage_data_artifacts(   stage_dir = "data/derived/imputation",   stage = "03_imputation" )

title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: clinical trials, electronic health records (EHR), epidemiological registries, data cleanliness rarely given. Datasets frequently exhibit complex missingness patterns, non-standard missing codes (e.g. "999", "-99", "Unknown", "Refused", ""), extreme statistical outliers data-entry errors severe disease phenotypes. Standard data science tools often assume missingness cleanly represented NA, requiring destructive multi-pass preprocessing exploratory analysis can even begin. TempleCBE package provides domain-tailored biostatistical tools audit non-standard missingness non-destructively, rank feature completeness, standardize numerical features, classify clinical outliers formal IQR standards, transition seamlessly tuned machine-learning imputation.

what: Existing tools and their limitations in clinical workflows
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: naniar & visdat: Pioneered tidy representation visualization missing data (vis_miss(), gg_miss_var()). However, operate exclusively existing NA values. raw clinical data contains sentinel values ("999", "-99", blank strings), users must first apply mutating functions like replace_with_na_all(), can accidentally alter legitimate numerical values, modify factor levels, mutate data types. mice / Amelia: Primarily multiple imputation engines. include basic diagnostics (e.g. md.pattern()), tools oriented toward parameter checking rather automated feature-level reporting regulatory deliverables. Base R / dplyr summaries: Simple calls like colSums(.na(df)) provide quick counts, lack built-percentage calculations, descending order sorting, sentinel code awareness, publication-ready formatting.

what: 1. Starting with a Full Synthetic Clinical Cohort
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: demonstrate missingness auditing empirically evaluate imputation accuracy, begin relatively full synthetic cohort N=120N = 120 clinical patients. real-world studies, true underlying values unknown lost. generating complete cohort realistic physiological correlations first, establish verifiable ground truth enables downstream recovery benchmarking: dataset contains: - Continuous biomarkers: age, systolic_bp, bmi, cholesterol, glucose. - Categorical clinical factors: smoker, hypertension, disease_stage. - Unique identifier: patient_id.
code: set.seed(2026) n <- 120  # Realistic clinical covariance structure age <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 58, sd = 9)) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 27.0, sd = 3.8), 1) systolic_bp <- round(95 + 0.45 * age + 0.65 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 7)) cholesterol <- round(155 + 0.55 * age + 1.10 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 15)) glucose <- round(72 + 0.35 * age + 0.95 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 10)) smoker <- factor(sample(c("No", "Yes"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.65, 0.35))) hypertension <- factor(ifelse(systolic_bp >= 135 | (age >= 62 & bmi >= 28), "Yes", "No")) disease_stage <- factor(sample(c("Stage I", "Stage II", "Stage III", "Stage IV"), n,   replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.30, 0.30, 0.25, 0.15) ))  cohort_clean <- tibble::tibble(   patient_id    = sprintf("PT_%03d", seq_len(n)),   age           = age,   systolic_bp   = systolic_bp,   bmi           = bmi,   cholesterol   = cholesterol,   glucose       = glucose,   smoker        = smoker,   hypertension  = hypertension,   disease_stage = disease_stage )  # Preview the clean cohort head(cohort_clean, 6) #> # A tibble: 6 × 9 #>   patient_id   age systolic_bp   bmi cholesterol glucose smoker hypertension #>   <chr>      <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl> <fct>  <fct>        #> 1 PT_001        63         147  34.2         244     133 Yes    Yes          #> 2 PT_002        48         140  35.1         189     134 No     Yes          #> 3 PT_003        59         148  27.9         187     117 No     Yes          #> 4 PT_004        57         146  30.4         200     111 No     Yes          #> 5 PT_005        52         132  20.4         222     128 No     No           #> 6 PT_006        35         129  28.8         219     128 Yes    No           #> # ℹ 1 more variable: disease_stage <fct>  # Verify complete data integrity (zero missingness) SumNa(cohort_clean) #> [1] 0

what: Heterogeneous missingness: Column-specific proportions via vector pct_na
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: real-world clinical cohorts, different variables rarely share identical missingness rate. Routine clinical covariates (age bmi) may missing 5–10% records, whereas specialized laboratory panels (cholesterol glucose) may uncollected 25–35% patients. add_missing() supports numeric vector pct_na whose length matches number selected columns: Notice features_percent_miss() directly reflects column’s distinct amputation share, missing_cells attribute accurately tracks varying number masked cells per feature.
code: # Generate column-specific missingness proportions with runif() set.seed(42) cols_ampute <- c("age", "systolic_bp", "bmi", "cholesterol", "glucose", "smoker", "hypertension")  p_vector <- cols_ampute |>   length() |>   runif(min = 0.05, max = 0.30) |>   round(2)  names(p_vector) <- cols_ampute p_vector #>          age  systolic_bp          bmi  cholesterol      glucose       smoker  #>         0.28         0.28         0.12         0.26         0.21         0.18  #> hypertension  #>         0.23  # Amputate each column according to its specific proportion amputed_hetero <- add_missing(   cohort_clean,   cols = c(age, systolic_bp, bmi, cholesterol, glucose, smoker, hypertension),   pct_na = p_vector )  # Inspect how features_percent_miss captures the heterogeneous rates features_percent_miss(amputed_hetero) #> # A tibble: 9 × 5 #>   feature       SumNa SumComp PctNa PctComp #>   <chr>         <int>   <int> <dbl>   <dbl> #> 1 age              34      86 0.283   0.717 #> 2 systolic_bp      34      86 0.283   0.717 #> 3 cholesterol      31      89 0.258   0.742 #> 4 hypertension     28      92 0.233   0.767 #> 5 glucose          25      95 0.208   0.792 #> 6 smoker           22      98 0.183   0.817 #> 7 bmi              14     106 0.117   0.883 #> 8 patient_id        0     120 0       1     #> 9 disease_stage     0     120 0       1

previous_headings: 5. Tuned Random Forest Imputation with missforest_sweep_mtry()
what: The mtry dilemma in clinical data
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: Random forest imputation iterates variable missing values, fitting forest predicting variable variables. single impactful hyperparameter mtry — number candidate variables sampled split: - mtry low, strong predictive biomarkers may missed key splits. - mtry high, trees become correlated overfit noisy clinical features. Critically, different clinical variables perform best different mtry values. continuous biomarker (e.g. systolic_bp) may achieve minimal error mtry=3mtry = 3, whereas binary factor (e.g. smoker) may perform best mtry=1mtry = 1. Standard implementations force analysts choose single global mtry.

previous_headings: 5. Tuned Random Forest Imputation with missforest_sweep_mtry()
what: TempleCBE’s solution: Independent per-column best mtry assembly
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: missforest_sweep_mtry() sweeps across candidate mtry values, tracks --bag (OOB) error every column every mtry, pulls column independently specific run column achieved minimal error.
code: # Run missForest sweep across mtry = 1:4 # We exclude patient_id and disease_stage from imputation predictors res_forest <- missforest_sweep_mtry(   data            = amputed,   exclude         = c("patient_id", "disease_stage"),   mtry_values     = 1:4,   ntree           = 60,   maxiter         = 5,   parallel        = FALSE,   seed            = 123 )

text: Survival analysis prognostic modeling R supported several foundational packages, including survival, glmnet, tidymodels (censored, yardstick), specialized evaluation packages like pec survAUC. However, applying frameworks real-world clinical cohorts longitudinal visits, time-dependent covariates, multi-center structures reveals substantial hurdles:

what: Existing tools and their limitations in longitudinal clinical modeling
title: Penalized Cox Models and Nested Cross-Validation for Start/Stop Survival Data
text: survival (Therneau): foundational baseline semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards Kaplan-Meier estimation. excellent classical low-dimensional epidemiological inference, lacks high-dimensional regularization (lasso, elastic net), automated cross-validation, tidy resampling integration. Data leakage start/stop data: cv.glmnet constructs folds randomly partitioning individual rows. counting-process data (Surv(tstart, tstop, status)), splits intervals belonging patient across training validation folds, leaking patient identity future biomarker trajectory validation set. cluster/site-level grouping: hold entire clinical sites hospital clusters evaluate generalizability across centers. Suboptimal metric selection: chooses penalty parameter λ\lambda using partial likelihood deviance Harrell’s C-index, without support time-dependent calibration, Integrated Brier Scores (IBS), IPCW adjustments. modern formula/recipe preprocessing: Predictors must supplied raw numeric design matrix (xx), forcing manual one-hot encoding outside cross-validation loop. Silent scoring failures: yardstick survival metrics expect one row per subject right-censored truth (Surv(time, event)). provided counting-process intervals (Surv(tstart, tstop, event)), yardstick returns numbers without error, silently treats every interval independent patient, biasing Brier scores ROC AUCs. Missing integrated nested CV penalized Cox: Evaluating regularized Cox models across α\alpha-mixture λ\lambda-penalty grid subject-level IPCW weights requires bespoke orchestration. pec / riskRegression / survAUC: Provide inverse-probability--censoring weights prediction error curves, operate standalone legacy systems decoupled recipes preprocessing tidymodels grammar.

title: Penalized Cox Models and Nested Cross-Validation for Start/Stop Survival Data
text: Clinical prognostic modeling frequently involves datasets dozens continuous lab values (e.g. creatinine, bilirubin, blood pressure) alongside categorical clinical indicators (e.g. disease stage, smoking status, sex, treatment center). Standard Principal Component Analysis ([recipes::step_pca()]) operates numeric columns; dummy-encoding categorical variables PCA distorts geometric distances binary indicators different variances continuous variables. step_famd() provides native recipes step Factor Analysis Mixed Data (Pagès 2004, implemented via FactoMineR::FAMD): - Continuous variables normalized unit variance. - Categorical variables dummy-coded weighted inversely category frequencies, ensuring variable contributes proportionally regardless number levels. step_famd() integrates directly cv_coxnet() nested_cv_coxnet(), ensuring components learned strictly inside training fold without leakage.
code: library(recipes)  # Define clinical recipe with mixed numeric and categorical predictors mixed_rec <- recipe(surv ~ age + bmi + marker + treatment + site + patient_id, data = sim_data) |>   update_role(patient_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Apply FAMD to compress continuous and discrete predictors into 3 components   step_famd(age, bmi, marker, treatment, site, num_comp = 3, prefix = "FAMD_")  # Train and inspect component contributions prepped_famd <- prep(mixed_rec, training = sim_data) baked_features <- bake(prepped_famd, new_data = NULL) head(baked_features)  # Inspect variance explained by components tidy(prepped_famd, number = 1, type = "variance")

what: Introduction: Dimension Reduction in Clinical and Exploratory Data Analysis
title: 07. Principal Component Analysis in R and SAS
text: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) unsupervised machine learning exploratory data analysis (EDA) technique widely utilized across biostatistics, clinical trials, epidemiological research. analyzing large cohorts extensive clinical measurements—repeated physiological scores, biomarker panels, intensive care metrics—investigators often face high dimensionality severe multicollinearity. summarized biostatistician Darina Chudnovskaya: “put simply, just think principal components new axes provide best angle see evaluate data, differences observations better visible.” — Darina Chudnovskaya (citing builtin.com) PCA reduces dimensionality multivariate continuous datasets transforming correlated variables smaller set uncorrelated, orthogonal variables known Principal Components (PCs). principal component linear combination original variables, structured : 1. first principal component (PC1PC_1) captures maximum possible variance data. 2. subsequent component (PC2,PC3,…PC_2, PC_3, \dots) captures maximum possible remaining variance mathematical constraint orthogonal (uncorrelated) preceding components. 3. total variance across principal components equals total variance original variables. principal components linear combinations may single physical unit measurement, analyzing loadings (eigenvectors) eigenvalues reveals underlying data structures, detects clustering, helps researchers select representative covariates downstream multivariable survival modeling (cbe_cox_multi()).

title: 07. Principal Component Analysis in R and SAS
text: mathematical execution PCA proceeds five fundamental steps: Standardize Variables: PCA sensitive measurement scales (variables larger numerical ranges spuriously dominate variance), features centered mean zero (μ=0\mu = 0) scaled unit variance (σ=1\sigma = 1): zij=xij−x‾jsjz_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j}{s_j} Standardizing mathematically equivalent performing PCA correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} rather unscaled covariance matrix 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma}. Calculate Correlation / Covariance Matrix: symmetric p×pp \times p correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} computed, capturing pairwise linear relationships correlation directions (+1+1 −1-1). Calculate Eigenvalues Eigenvectors: Eigen-decomposition solves characteristic equation: det⁡(𝐑−λ𝐈)=0⟹𝐑𝐯k=λk𝐯k\det(\mathbf{R} - \lambda \mathbf{}) = 0 \quad \implies \quad \mathbf{R} \mathbf{v}_k = \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k Eigenvalues (λk\lambda_k): Represent variance explained kk-th principal component. standardized PCA pp variables, ∑k=1pλk=p\sum_{k=1}^p \lambda_k = p. Eigenvectors (𝐯k\mathbf{v}_k): Unit-length directional vectors defining principal axes (loadings). Select Principal Components: Kaiser-Guttman Criterion: Retain components eigenvalues λk≥1\lambda_k \ge 1 (explaining variance individual original standardized variable). Scree Plot Elbow: Identify inflection point additional components yield diminishing marginal variance. Cumulative Variance Threshold: Retain enough components explain pre-specified proportion variance (typically 70%–80%). Recast Observations onto Principal Component Axes: Observations projected onto retained eigenvectors generate principal component scores: 𝐘=𝐙𝐕k\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_k

code: """ Python script: Call TempleCBE LOCO-MP Cox model via rpy2 """ import numpy as np import pandas as pd import rpy2.robjects as ro from rpy2.robjects import pandas2ri from rpy2.robjects.packages import importr  # Activate automated Pandas <-> R DataFrame conversion pandas2ri.activate()  # Import TempleCBE and survival packages templecbe = importr('TempleCBE') survival = importr('survival') base = importr('base')  # 1. Load or simulate survival data in Python n = 120 data_py = pd.DataFrame({     'time': np.random.exponential(scale=10, size=n) + 1,     'status': np.random.binomial(1, 0.65, size=n),     'age': np.random.normal(55, 10, size=n),     'biomarker_a': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'biomarker_b': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'noise_1': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'noise_2': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n) })  # 2. Convert Pandas DataFrame to R DataFrame data_r = pandas2ri.py2rpy(data_py)  # 3. Fit LOCO-MP Penalized Cox Model in TempleCBE fit_r = templecbe.cbe_loco_mp_coxnet(     formula = ro.Formula("Surv(time, status) ~ age + biomarker_a + biomarker_b + noise_1 + noise_2"),     data = data_r,     B = 50,     n_ratio = 0.7,     m_ratio = 0.5,     seed = 42 )  # 4. Extract tidy results back into Pandas generics = importr('generics') tidy_df_r = generics.tidy(fit_r) tidy_df_py = pandas2ri.rpy2py(tidy_df_r)  print("--- TempleCBE LOCO-MP Results in Python ---") print(tidy_df_py[['term', 'importance', 'std_error', 'statistic', 'p_adjusted', 'conf_low', 'conf_high']])

For each one-unit increase in age, the risk of the event increases by 1.9%. The p-value indicates that this association is statistically significant. res_age$zph_table #>            chisq df         p #> age    0.3434595  1 0.5578391 #> GLOBAL 0.3434595  1 0.5578391 cat(res_age$zph_text) #> Test of the proportional hazards assumption yields p = 0.558. Therefore, the proportional hazards assumption is not violated.

text: Cohort: 45 rodents exposed carcinogen randomized three dose levels tumor-promoting agent (Dose: 1.0, 2.5, 10.0). Time-Dependent Predictor: Number papillomas (NPap), observed repeatedly across 15 scheduled observation times (weeks 27, 34, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 65, 67, 71). Outcome: Death (Dead = 1) censoring (Dead = 0) Time. raw data structured wide format columns P1 P15 indicating papilloma counts 15 measurement weeks:

title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: SAS, repeated measurements can handled either programming statements transforming data counting-process format (Tumor1), animal multiple intervals (T1, T2] corresponding time segments NPap remained constant: TempleCBE implements exact DATA step algorithm tumor_long(): Let us examine Subject 1, animal died week 47 increasing papilloma counts time: published SAS documentation, Subject 1 produces exactly 5 intervals: (0, 27, 0, 0), (27, 34, 5, 0), (34, 37, 6, 0), (37, 41, 8, 0), (41, 47, 10, 1).
code: /* SAS Counting-Process Transformation (Example 85.7) */ data Tumor1(keep=ID Time Dead Dose T1 T2 NPap Status);    array pp{*} P1-P14;    array qq{*} P2-P15;    array tt{1:15} _temporary_       (27 34 37 41 43 45 46 47 49 50 51 53 65 67 71);    set Tumor;    T1 = 0; T2 = 0; Status = 0;    if ( Time = tt[1] ) then do;       T2 = tt[1]; NPap = p1; Status = Dead; output;    end;    else do _i_=1 to dim(pp);       if ( tt[_i_] = Time ) then do;          T2 = Time; NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = Dead; output;       end;       else if (tt[_i_] < Time ) then do;          if (pp[_i_] ^= qq[_i_] ) then do;             if qq[_i_] = . then T2 = Time;             else                T2 = tt[_i_];             NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = 0; output;             T1 = T2;          end;       end;    end;    if ( Time >= tt[15] ) then do;       T2 = Time; NPap = P15; Status = Dead; output;    end; run; l <- TempleCBE:::tumor_long(w) dim(l) #> [1] 102   8 filter(l, ID == 1) #> # A tibble: 5 × 8 #>      ID  Time  Dead  Dose    T1    T2  NPap Status #>   <int> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1     1    47     1     1     0    27     0      0 #> 2     1    47     1     1    27    34     5      0 #> 3     1    47     1     1    34    37     6      0 #> 4     1    47     1     1    37    41     8      0 #> 5     1    47     1     1    41    47    10      1

text: SAS clinical programming, transforming repeated biomarker panels counting-process layouts often relies complex, verbose DATA-step macros temporary arrays, lag lookups, index boundaries. R provides modern, elegant alternatives.

previous_headings: Part 3: Time-Dependent Merging: SAS DATA Step vs. survival::tmerge vs. tidy_tmerge_cox
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: Therneau’s survival::tmerge constructs start-stop survival intervals combining baseline cohort data sequential event time-dependent covariate tables: Comparing fitted coefficients tmerge SAS DATA-step Tumor1 data: models identical 10−1710^{-17}! SAS DATA step collapsed adjacent intervals identical values (resulting 102 rows), tmerge splits observation time (resulting 412 rows). hazard risk set contributions intervals unchanged covariates identical, partial likelihood resulting estimates match exactly.
code: # 1. Base cohort with primary follow-up interval and event status base_df <- w %>% select(ID, Time, Dead, Dose)  tumor_tmerge <- tmerge(   data1 = base_df,   data2 = base_df,   id = ID,   Status = event(Time, Dead) )  # 2. Extract longitudinal transitions: at each observation time, update NPap tt <- c(27, 34, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 65, 67, 71) transitions <- list() for (r in seq_len(nrow(w))) {   id_i <- w$ID[r]   tm_i <- w$Time[r]   p_vals <- as.numeric(w[r, paste0("P", 1:15)])   transitions[[length(transitions) + 1]] <- data.frame(ID = id_i, time = 0, NPap = p_vals[1])   for (k in 1:14) {     if (tt[k] < tm_i && !is.na(p_vals[k + 1])) {       transitions[[length(transitions) + 1]] <- data.frame(ID = id_i, time = tt[k], NPap = p_vals[k + 1])     }   } } tdc_df <- bind_rows(transitions)  # 3. Apply time-dependent covariate update via tmerge tumor_tmerge <- tmerge(   data1 = tumor_tmerge,   data2 = tdc_df,   id = ID,   NPap = tdc(time, NPap) )  # Fit Cox model on tmerge data fit_tmerge <- cbe_cox_multi(   data = tumor_tmerge,   formula = Surv(tstart, tstop, Status) ~ Dose + NPap,   id = ID,   ties = "breslow" ) coef(fit_tmerge$model) #>       Dose       NPap  #> 0.06885124 0.11715304 coef(fit_tumor$model) #>       Dose       NPap  #> 0.06885124 0.11715304  # Difference down to machine precision: max(abs(coef(fit_tmerge$model) - coef(fit_tumor$model))) #> [1] 4.163336e-17

code: # Example longitudinal biomarker measurements measurements <- tibble::tibble(   subject_id = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2),   time       = c(0, 20, 40, 0, 30),   biomarker  = c(1.2, 1.5, 1.8, 0.9, 1.1) )  # Endpoint table endpoints <- tibble::tibble(   subject_id = c(1, 2),   event_time = c(50, 60),   event_type = c("Death", "Censored") )  # Baseline covariates baseline <- tibble::tibble(   subject_id = c(1, 2),   age        = c(55, 62),   arm        = c("Active", "Control") )  # One-step tidy construction tidy_surv <- tidy_tmerge_cox(   measure_df = measurements,   event_df = endpoints,   baseline_df = baseline,   id = "subject_id",   measure_time = "time",   event_time = "event_time",   event_type = "event_type" )  tidy_surv #> # A tibble: 5 × 11 #>   subject_id  time biomarker event_time event_type   age arm     tstart tstop #>        <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> #> 1          1     0       1.2         50 Death         55 Active       0    20 #> 2          1    20       1.5         50 Death         55 Active      20    40 #> 3          1    40       1.8         50 Death         55 Active      40    50 #> 4          2     0       0.9         60 Censored      62 Control      0    30 #> 5          2    30       1.1         60 Censored      62 Control     30    60 #> # ℹ 2 more variables: event <dbl>, event_label <chr> cbe_cox_multi(   data = tidy_surv,   formula = Surv(tstart, tstop, event) ~ biomarker + age + arm,   id = subject_id )

what: Part 4: Model Calibration & Integrated Brier Score (IBS) Parity
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: clinical risk prediction, model discrimination (Harrell’s CC-index) evaluates relative ordering, fails assess whether predicted absolute probabilities match observed clinical outcomes. Proper scoring rules—specifically Brier score Integrated Brier Score (IBS)—quantify mean squared prediction error right censoring.

previous_headings: Part 4: Model Calibration & Integrated Brier Score (IBS) Parity
what: 4.1 Theoretical Foundation: IPCW Brier Score & IBS (Graf et al. 1999)
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: specific evaluation time horizon tt, Brier score measures squared difference true binary survival status (Ti>t)(T_i > t) predicted survival probability Ŝ(t∣Xi)\hat{S}(t \mid X_i). prevent bias censored individuals whose status tt unknown, Graf et al. (1999) weight observations Inverse Probability Censoring Weights (IPCW): BS(t)=1N∑=1Nwi(t)⋅[(Ti>t)−Ŝ(t∣Xi)]2BS(t) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{=1}^N w_i(t) \cdot \left[ (T_i > t) - \hat{S}(t \mid X_i) \right]^2 IPCW weight wi(t)w_i(t) derived Kaplan-Meier estimate censoring distribution Ĝ(u)=P(C>u)\hat{G}(u) = P(C > u): wi(t)={1Ĝ(t),Ti>t(subject remains risk)1Ĝ(Ti−),Ti≤t δi=1(observed event time t)0,Ti≤t δi=0(censored prior time t)w_i(t) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\hat{G}(t)}, & \text{} T_i > t \quad (\text{subject remains risk}) \\ \frac{1}{\hat{G}(T_i^-)}, & \text{} T_i \le t \text{ } \delta_i = 1 \quad (\text{observed event time } t) \\ 0, & \text{} T_i \le t \text{ } \delta_i = 0 \quad (\text{censored prior time } t) \end{cases} summarize overall model accuracy across entire follow-horizon [tmin,tmax][t_{\min}, t_{\max}], Integrated Brier Score (IBS) integrates time-dependent Brier loss using trapezoidal rule: IBS=1tmax∫0tmaxBS(t)dt≈1tK∑k=1K−1BS(tk)+BS(tk+1)2⋅(tk+1−tk)\text{IBS} = \frac{1}{t_{\max}} \int_0^{t_{\max}} BS(t) \, dt \approx \frac{1}{t_K} \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \frac{BS(t_k) + BS(t_{k+1})}{2} \cdot (t_{k+1} - t_k)

what: 4.2 TempleCBE Implementation on NCCTG Lung Cancer Cohort
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: TempleCBE, survival predictions scored using censoring_km(), add_graf_weights(), yardstick::brier_survival():
code: # Filter complete cases for the multivariable model lung_complete <- lung_data %>%   filter(!is.na(ph.karno))  # 1. Fit multivariable Cox model with Breslow tie handling (matching SAS default) fit_calib <- cbe_cox_multi(   data = lung_complete,   formula = Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.karno,   ties = "breslow" )  # 2. Extract predicted survival curves at milestone evaluation times (100 to 500 days) eval_horizons <- c(100, 200, 300, 400, 500) sfit <- survfit(fit_calib$model, newdata = lung_complete) surv_mat <- summary(sfit, times = eval_horizons)$surv  # Construct per-subject prediction list for yardstick pred_list <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(lung_complete)), function(i) {   tibble::tibble(     .eval_time = eval_horizons,     .pred_survival = surv_mat[, i]   ) })  scored_lung <- tibble::tibble(   .truth = Surv(lung_complete$time, lung_complete$status),   .pred = pred_list )  # 3. Add Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights (IPCW) scored_lung <- add_graf_weights(   scored_lung,   censoring = censoring_km(Surv(lung_complete$time, lung_complete$status)) )  # 4. Compute time-dependent Brier scores and Integrated Brier Score (IBS) brier_res <- yardstick::brier_survival(scored_lung, truth = .truth, .pred) ibs_res <- yardstick::brier_survival_integrated(scored_lung, truth = .truth, .pred)  brier_res #> # A tibble: 5 × 4 #>   .metric        .estimator .eval_time .estimate #>   <chr>          <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 brier_survival standard          100     0.113 #> 2 brier_survival standard          200     0.201 #> 3 brier_survival standard          300     0.230 #> 4 brier_survival standard          400     0.227 #> 5 brier_survival standard          500     0.200 ibs_res #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   .metric                   .estimator .estimate #>   <chr>                     <chr>          <dbl> #> 1 brier_survival_integrated standard       0.163

code: # Extract 300-day predicted survival p300 <- surv_mat[3, ] lung_complete$pred_surv_300 <- p300 lung_complete$quintile <- dplyr::ntile(lung_complete$pred_surv_300, 5)  # Calculate observed Kaplan-Meier within each predicted quintile at t = 300 calib_df <- lung_complete %>%   group_by(quintile) %>%   summarize(     n = n(),     mean_pred = mean(pred_surv_300),     obs_km = {       km <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1)       summary(km, times = 300, extend = TRUE)$surv     },     .groups = "drop"   )  # Calibration plot with 45-degree reference line ggplot(calib_df, aes(x = mean_pred, y = obs_km)) +   geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +   geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#8B1E41", alpha = 0.85) +   geom_line(color = "#8B1E41", linewidth = 0.8) +   scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 0.9), labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +   scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 0.9), labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +   labs(     title = "Model Calibration at 300 Days (NCCTG Lung Cohort)",     subtitle = "Observed Kaplan-Meier survival vs. Mean predicted survival across risk quintiles",     x = "Mean Predicted Survival Probability",     y = "Observed Kaplan-Meier Survival Rate",     size = "Patients"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

what: 5.5 End-to-End Hybrid Workflow: Calling a SAS Macro from R (R →\rightarrow SAS →\rightarrow R)
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: many clinical environments, analysts want call validated SAS macro directly R data frame without manually writing standalone SAS programs hand. complete round-trip pattern consists four steps: 1. Export Cohort R: Write R dataset FDA standard transport format (haven::write_xpt()). 2. Compose SAS Macro Driver: Generate lightweight .sas script invoking bundled macro (e.g. %cbe_brier_score). 3. Execute via run_sas_script(): Run SAS batch mode, generating audit logs listing tables. 4. Import Results R: Read generated SAS dataset (haven::read_sas()) back R tibble visualization verification.
code: # 1. Prepare R analysis cohort and export to FDA Transport format lung_xpt_data <- lung_data %>%   filter(!is.na(ph.karno)) %>%   rename(ph_karno = ph.karno) %>%   select(time, status, age, sex, ph_karno)  work_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "cbe_sas_job") dir.create(work_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) xpt_path <- file.path(work_dir, "lung.xpt") driver_path <- file.path(work_dir, "run_brier_macro.sas") out_brier_path <- file.path(work_dir, "sas_brier.sas7bdat") out_ibs_path <- file.path(work_dir, "sas_ibs.sas7bdat")  # Export to standard SAS Version 5 XPORT format (member name <= 8 chars) haven::write_xpt(lung_xpt_data, xpt_path, version = 5, name = "LUNG")  # 2. Dynamically compose SAS driver invoking %cbe_brier_score macro_file <- TempleCBE::cbe_sas_macro_path("cbe_brier_score.sas")  driver_code <- sprintf(' libname workdir "%s"; libname xfile xport "%s";  /* Copy transport file into SAS WORK library */ proc copy in=xfile out=work; run;  /* Include TempleCBE macro */ %%include "%s";  /* Execute macro */ %%cbe_brier_score(     data       = work.lung,     time       = time,     status     = status,     pred_vars  = age sex ph_karno,     eval_times = 100 200 300 400 500,     ties       = BRESLOW,     trunc      = 0.05,     out_brier  = workdir.sas_brier,     out_ibs    = workdir.sas_ibs ); ', gsub("\\\\", "/", work_dir), gsub("\\\\", "/", xpt_path), gsub("\\\\", "/", macro_file))  writeLines(driver_code, driver_path)  # 3. Execute SAS batch job from R status <- TempleCBE::run_sas_script(driver_path) cat("SAS Macro Execution Status:", status, "\n")  # 4. Import SAS output dataset directly back into R sas_brier_tbl <- haven::read_sas(out_brier_path) sas_ibs_tbl <- haven::read_sas(out_ibs_path)  # 5. Display SAS macro results inside R sas_ibs_tbl dplyr::distinct(sas_brier_tbl, eval_time, brier_score)

However, longitudinal biomarker trajectories measured biological noise subject informative dropout, treating fixed step-functions introduces attenuation bias (Rizopoulos 2010, JSS 35(9); Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos 2018, JSS 84(12)). address : - SAS: Biostatisticians employ %JM macro, fitting joint generalized linear mixed model (PROC NLMIXED adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature) proportional hazards model. - TempleCBE: Analysts deploy joint_model() proc_contents(), fit coordinated survival (coxnet), binary classification (status), duration regression (time) models integrated probability calibration:
code: # Audit dataset with repeated-measures detection toy_long <- data.frame(   patid = rep(1:20, each = 3),   tstart = rep(c(0, 5, 10), times = 20),   tstop = rep(c(5, 10, 20), times = 20),   biomarker = rnorm(60, mean = 50, sd = 10),   trt = rep(sample(c("A", "B"), 20, replace = TRUE), each = 3),   status = rep(rbinom(20, 1, 0.5), each = 3) ) toy_long$surv <- survival::Surv(toy_long$tstart, toy_long$tstop, toy_long$status)  # Audit counting-process duration and baseline vs longitudinal features audit_res <- proc_contents(toy_long, subject_id = "patid") audit_res[, c("columns", "class", "variable_type", "mean", "most_freq")] #> # A tibble: 7 × 5 #>   columns   class     variable_type                mean most_freq                #>   <chr>     <chr>     <chr>                       <dbl> <chr>                    #> 1 patid     integer   Subject ID                  10.5  1                        #> 2 tstart    numeric   Longitudinal (Time-Varying)  5    0                        #> 3 tstop     numeric   Longitudinal (Time-Varying) 11.7  5                        #> 4 biomarker numeric   Longitudinal (Time-Varying) 49.4  25.6273638878047         #> 5 trt       character Baseline (Time-Invariant)   NA    A                        #> 6 status    integer   Baseline (Time-Invariant)    0.5  0                        #> 7 surv      Surv      Longitudinal (Time-Varying)  6.67 Counting (Events: 30 [5…  # Fit joint multi-paradigm predictive model jm_fit <- joint_model(toy_long, surv ~ biomarker + trt, subject_id = "patid", penalty = 0.05) print(jm_fit) #> === TempleCBE Joint Survival-Status-Time Model === #> Engine: glmnet | Calibration: TRUE #> Outcome: surv (Type: counting) #> Sample Size: 60 observations | Predictors: 5 #> Events: 30 (50.0%) | Median Follow-up Time: 10.00 #> Fitted Sub-Models: #>   1. title: FilePath S4 Class — FilePath-class
text: Represents individual file node computational pipeline dependency graph. FilePath object encapsulates file-level metadata state: tracking modification timestamps (mtime), file extensions (file_ext), workflow lifecycle milestones (stage), semantic pipeline roles (artifact_role), rendering status (renders). Upon instantiation, object automatically inspects target file disk: file exists path, mtime populated file.info()$mtime file_ext extracted via tools::file_ext().

title: FilePath S4 Class — FilePath-class
text: name Character. user-supplied, human-readable name file, used refer file across parts pipeline dependency graph. path Character. absolute project-relative path file file system. mtime POSIXct. modification time file file system. Automatically populated disk object initialization file exists. file_ext Character. file extension file (e.g., "xlsx", "rds", "qmd"). Automatically populated file path object initialization. renders Logical. logical indicating whether file rendered file (.e. file produced rendering process) rendering source script. Defaults FALSE. stage Character. workflow lifecycle stage file pipeline (e.g., "01_EDA", "02_Analysis_Original", "03_Imputation"). artifact_role Character. semantic role file pipeline. Standard roles include: "raw_data": Original immutable input data (e.g. source spreadsheets). "derived_data": Primary processed baseline dataset generated raw inputs. "enhanced_data": Imputed augmented analytical dataset. "intermediate_data": Stage-internal calculation artifact model. "report_source": Executable source document (e.g., Quarto .qmd). "deliverable_report": Rendered deliverable (e.g., .pdf, .html). "helper_script": Child modular helper script invoked parent reports. "reference": Lookup tables, crosswalks, project configuration files. description Character. brief human-readable description file's contents analytical purpose.

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
code: anonymize_pi(   name,   method = c("hmac_token", "hmac_surname", "token", "synthetic"),   key = Sys.getenv("TEMPLECBE_SECRET_KEY", unset = ""),   secrets_path = NULL,   exclude = character(),   prefix = "PI_",   n_chars = 16,   rename_fn = NULL,   seed = NULL )

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
text: name Character vector investigator names surnames mask. method Character string specifying anonymization approach: `"hmac_token"`, `"hmac_surname"`, `"token"`, `"synthetic"`. key Character string, secret key / pepper HMAC methods. Defaults `Sys.getenv("TEMPLECBE_SECRET_KEY", unset = "")`. secrets_path Path confidential mapping file `method = "token"`. Defaults `tools::R_user_dir("TempleCBE", = "data")/pi_mapping.json`. exclude Character vector names must never generated (passed [generate_last_names()] method `"hmac_surname"` `"synthetic"`). prefix Character string, prefix tokens (default `"PI_"`). n_chars Integer, number hex characters tokens (default 8). Can shortened short names. rename_fn Optional function rename format generated tokens/pseudonyms. seed Optional integer, random seed method `"synthetic"`.

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
text: Character vector anonymized tokens pseudonyms, matching length `name`.

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
text: Methods: `"hmac_token"` (default): Stateless deterministic token (e.g., `PI_5c1ebfd9`) computed via     `openssl::sha256(name, key = key)`. mapping file needed disk. `"hmac_surname"`: Stateless deterministic procedural surname generated via     keyed HMAC seed [generate_last_names()]. Consistent across runs without disk state. `"token"`: Stateful cryptographic tokens persisted user-level JSON mapping file     (`tools::R_user_dir("TempleCBE", "data")/pi_mapping.json`). Explicitly refuses write     Git repository tree prevent accidental commits PHI. `"synthetic"`: Random procedural surnames via [generate_last_names()].

title: Anonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
code: # Vectorized token mapping (default method = "hmac_token") anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor", "Patel"), key = "study_salt") #> [1] "PI_74a3a4218fa7aa9c" "PI_55cad5aeb6812bac" "PI_c4c136722bee9305"  # Short tokens (4 characters) anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), n_chars = 4, key = "study_salt") #> [1] "PI_74a3" "PI_55ca"  # Custom renaming function anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), rename_fn = tolower, key = "study_salt") #> [1] "pi_74a3a4218fa7aa9c" "pi_55cad5aeb6812bac"  # Vectorized realistic pseudonyms anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), method = "hmac_surname", key = "study_salt") #> [1] "Glasujoll" "Staroford"

title: Compare Two Data Frames (SAS PROC COMPARE Parity) — cbe_compare_df
text: base base data frame tibble (equivalent SAS base=). compare comparison data frame tibble (equivalent SAS compare=). Optional character vector column names specifying key variables used align observations across datasets (equivalent SAS id statement). NULL (default), observations compared row order. tolerance Non-negative numeric threshold numeric differences (default: 1e-7). Differences absolute magnitude less equal tolerance considered matches. base_name Optional character string identifying base dataset. NULL, deparsed base argument. compare_name Optional character string identifying comparison dataset. NULL, deparsed compare argument. max_diffs Maximum number discrepant rows store per variable (default: 100).

title: Compare Two Data Frames (SAS PROC COMPARE Parity) — cbe_compare_df
text: S3 object class "cbe_compare_df" containing: meta List containing metadata dataset names, dimensions, tolerance, keys. variables List elements common, base_only, compare_only. summary Tibble summarizing comparison status variable (types, match status, difference counts, max difference, RMSE). observations List summarizing observation matching (counts, keys matched, unmatched). diffs Tibble containing detailed cell--cell discrepancies variables exceeding tolerance. is_concordant Logical indicating whether datasets match completely within tolerance common variables observations.

title: Compare Two Data Frames (SAS PROC COMPARE Parity) — cbe_compare_df

title: Institutional Categorical Hypothesis Test for gtsummary and Batch Testing — cbe_test_categorical
text: function follows rigorous 4-rule hierarchy: 2x2 table zero cell: Uses Central Fisher's exact test     mid-p adjustment (exact2x2 midp = TRUE)     avoid extreme conservatism. 2x2 table without zero cell: Uses Central Fisher's exact test     (exact2x2 midp = FALSE). RxC table sparse counts: expected cell count     less 5, runs Fisher's exact test Monte Carlo simulation     (fisher.test simulate.p.value = TRUE). RxC table adequate counts: expected cell counts     least 5, runs Pearson's Chi-squared test without continuity correction     (chisq.test correct = FALSE).

Group coarser unit, study site, leave-sites-cross-validation; subject must belong one group. **Fitting.** `mixture`, one penalty path computed `data` (`cv.glmnet()` ) every fold fit along . recipe, recipe prepped analysis set, preprocessing learned inside fold. **Predictions.** Survival assessment-set subject computed Breslow baseline hazard analysis set. `covariates = "path"`, cumulative hazard integrated subject's start/stop covariate path, carrying interval's values forward next interval past last one; `"baseline"`, covariates first interval used, uses information time 0. static concordance metric uses predicted survival last `eval_time`. **Scoring.** Start/stop rows collapsed one row per subject ([surv_subject_truth()]), weighted censoring Graf weights analysis set ([graf_weights()]), passed `metrics`. **Selection.** `lambda.min` penalty, across `mixture` values, best mean `metric` folds (time-specific metrics, first `eval_time`). `lambda.1se` largest penalty, mixture, whose mean within one standard error best mean.

code: # \donttest{ if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("rsample", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("yardstick", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   # Start/stop data: up to 3 visits per subject, events only at the last one   long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:80, function(i) {     k <- sample(1:3, 1)     stops <- cumsum(stats::runif(k, 2, 6))     risk <- stats::rnorm(1)     data.frame(subject_id = i, tstart = c(0, utils::head(stops, -1)), tstop = stops,                status = c(rep(0, k - 1), stats::rbinom(1, 1, stats::plogis(risk))),                x1 = risk + stats::rnorm(k, sd = 0.2), x2 = stats::rnorm(k), x3 = stats::rnorm(k))   }))   cv <- cv_coxnet(     survival::Surv(tstart, tstop, status) ~ x1 + x2 + x3,     data = long, subject_id = "subject_id", mixture = c(0.5, 1),     v = 5, nlambda = 20, cox.ties = "breslow"   )   cv   generics::tidy(cv, penalty = "lambda.1se") } #> # A tibble: 3 × 3 #>   term  estimate penalty #>   <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl> #> 1 x1       0.333   0.105 #> 2 x2       0       0.105 #> 3 x3       0       0.105 # }

title: Integrated Brier Score of a Penalized Cox Model on Start/Stop Survival Data — glmnet_IBS
text: object `rsplit` (e.g. one element `rsample` resamples). alpha Elastic net mixing parameter: 1 lasso, 0 ridge. recipe unprepped [recipes::recipe()]. feature_names Character vector baked predictor column names, function takes baked analysis set returns – recipes whose output columns vary fold, `step_pca(threshold = )`. time_data Optional data frame columns `start_col` `stop_col`; positive stop times used `eval_time` `NULL`. formula Optional character string `+`-separated feature names (one-sided formula) restrict model subset `feature_names`. Defaults . internal_folds Number subject-grouped folds used choose penalty. id_col, start_col, stop_col, status_col Column names subject identifier, interval start, interval stop, event indicator (1 = event). censoring_weights `"ipcw"` supported. `"none"`, scored interval rows without adjusting censoring, removed TempleCBE 0.3.0; install TempleCBE 0.2.0 reproduce results used . prep_on `"baseline"` (default) preps `recipe` subject's first interval analysis set; `""` preps every analysis row. eval_time Evaluation times IBS. Defaults stop times `time_data`, else deciles analysis-set event times. metric Name yardstick survival metric chooses penalty, e.g. `"brier_survival_integrated"` `"concordance_survival"`. rule `"min"` `"1se"`: report penalty `lambda.min` `lambda.1se`. covariates `"path"` `"baseline"`; see [cv_coxnet()]. failure_ibs IBS reported model fit (default `NA`); warning gives reason. ... arguments passed [glmnet::glmnet()], `cox.ties` (`"breslow"` `"efron"`). glmnet 5.0 defaults Breslow 5.1 Efron, pass `cox.ties` keep results stable across glmnet versions.

title: Integrated Brier Score of a Penalized Cox Model on Start/Stop Survival Data — glmnet_IBS
text: 1. **Preprocessing.** `recipe` prepped analysis set –    subject's first interval `prep_on = "baseline"` – baked onto    sets. recipe must keep `id_col`, `start_col`, `stop_col`,    `status_col` output (e.g. `"id variable"` role). 2. **Tuning.** [cv_coxnet()] chooses penalty baked analysis set    `internal_folds` folds grouped subject, `metric` (IBS    default). Earlier versions used [glmnet::cv.glmnet()], chose    penalty concordance folds rows, splitting subjects' intervals    folds. 3. **Scoring.** model, refit whole analysis set, predicts    assessment-set subject's survival analysis-set Breslow baseline    hazard along covariate path (see [cv_coxnet()]), scored    [yardstick::brier_survival_integrated()] inverse-probability--    censoring (Graf) weights estimated analysis set.

title: Integrated Brier Score of a Penalized Cox Model on Start/Stop Survival Data — glmnet_IBS
text: Graf E, Schmoor C, Sauerbrei W, Schumacher M (1999). Assessment   comparison prognostic classification schemes survival data.   *Statistics Medicine*, 18(17-18), 2529-2545.

title: Integrated Brier Score of a Penalized Cox Model on Start/Stop Survival Data — glmnet_IBS
code: # \donttest{ if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("yardstick", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("rsample", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   # Synthetic start/stop data: 60 subjects, up to 3 intervals each   long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:60, function(i) {     k <- sample(1:3, 1)     stops <- c(5, 10, 20)[1:k]     risk <- rnorm(1)     data.frame(subject_id = i, tstart = c(0, head(stops, -1)), tstop = stops,                status = c(rep(0, k - 1), rbinom(1, 1, plogis(risk))),                x1 = risk + rnorm(k, sd = 0.2), x2 = rnorm(k))   }))   rec <- recipes::recipe(~ ., data = long) |>     recipes::update_role(subject_id, tstart, tstop, status, new_role = "id variable") |>     recipes::step_range(recipes::all_numeric_predictors())   split <- rsample::group_initial_split(long, group = subject_id)   glmnet_IBS(split, alpha = 0.5, recipe = rec, feature_names = c("x1", "x2"),              time_data = unique(long[, c("tstart", "tstop")]), internal_folds = 3,              id_col = "subject_id", cox.ties = "breslow") } #> # A tibble: 2 × 5 #>     IBS lambda term  estimate alpha #>   <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 0.112 0.0746 x1           0   0.5 #> 2 0.112 0.0746 x2           0   0.5 # }

title: Test Whether a Vector Looks Poisson-Distributed — is_poisson
text: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test deliberately ** used : KS statistic's null distribution assumes continuous CDF, Poisson distribution discrete real point masses, inflates KS statistic (deflates p-value) regardless true fit — chi-squared test standard, correctly-calibrated tool discrete/count goodness--fit. is_normal uses Lilliefors variant Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, suits continuous normal distribution. code: # \donttest{ if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("rsample", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("yardstick", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:90, function(i) {     k <- sample(1:3, 1)     stops <- cumsum(stats::runif(k, 2, 6))     risk <- stats::rnorm(1)     data.frame(subject_id = i, tstart = c(0, utils::head(stops, -1)), tstop = stops,                status = c(rep(0, k - 1), stats::rbinom(1, 1, stats::plogis(risk))),                x1 = risk + stats::rnorm(k, sd = 0.2), x2 = stats::rnorm(k), x3 = stats::rnorm(k))   }))   folds <- rsample::nested_cv(     long,     outside = rsample::group_vfold_cv(group = subject_id, v = 3),     inside = rsample::group_vfold_cv(group = subject_id, v = 3)   )   res <- nested_cv_coxnet(     folds, survival::Surv(tstart, tstop, status) ~ x1 + x2 + x3,     subject_id = "subject_id", mixture = c(0.5, 1),     metrics = yardstick::metric_set(yardstick::brier_survival_integrated,                                     yardstick::concordance_survival),     nlambda = 20, cox.ties = "breslow"   )   res } #> # A tibble: 3 × 6 #>   id        mixture penalty .metrics         .coefs           .inner            #>   <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl> <list>           <list>           <list>            #> 1 Resample1     0.5  0.0193 <tibble [2 × 4]> <tibble [3 × 3]> <tibble [54 × 8]> #> 2 Resample2     1    0.0628 <tibble [2 × 4]> <tibble [3 × 3]> <tibble [54 × 8]> #> 3 Resample3     1    0.0447 <tibble [2 × 4]> <tibble [3 × 3]> <tibble [58 × 8]> # }

what: Exact Contingency Methods, Chi-Square Testing & Visualizations
title: TempleCBE 0.3.403
text: New cbe_exact2x2() performs exact inference using exact2x2. cell count 2x2 table zero (min(tab) == 0), automatically defaults mid-p version Central Fisher’s exact test (midp = TRUE), preventing extreme conditional conservatism. non-zero tables, defaults standard Central Fisher (midp = FALSE). New cbe_exact2x2_ci() generates publication-ready odds ratio confidence interval strings (e.g. "0.8 (0.3, 2.1)"). Added test = c("auto", "exact", "chisq", "fisher") correct = FALSE (uncorrected Pearson χ2\chi^2) cbe_test_categorical(), providing drop-custom test gtsummary::add_p() implementing institutional CBE testing guidelines. New cbe_four_quadrant_report() generates standard clinical 4-quadrant report (q1 | q2 // q3 | q4 // p = pformat) returning structured quadrant percentages, console-ready text cards, compact 3-line summaries, ggplot square tiles configurable test engines ("auto", "exact", "chisq", "fisher"). Dedicated wrapper cbe_square_plot() provides direct access 4-quadrant reports square glyph plots. New exported pformat() (alias cbe_pformat()) formats numeric p-values publication-ready strings (e.g. pformat(0.042) -> "p = 0.042", pformat(0.0001) -> "p < 0.001"). Unified contingency visualization supporting balloon, bar (fill, dodge, stack), mosaic, heatmap, square, corrplot automatic hypothesis test calculation (test = "auto", "exact", "chisq", "fisher"). New plot_categorical_associations() creates pairwise categorical correlation matrices using Cramér’s V −log⁡10(p)-\log_{10}(p) via corrplot Temple University brand palettes. New cbe_pairwise_combos() enumerates pairwise categorical combinations sequential indexing child-document expansion. Renamed primary function render() render_me preserved alias full backwards compatibility. Enhanced path parameter accept character vectors, lists paths, S4 compute graph objects (FileOutputs, FilePath), render plans get_render_plan(), full pipeline lists (automatic filtering renderable targets). Added ... forwarding pass options (params, execute_params, output_dir, quiet) cleanly quarto::quarto_render() rmarkdown::render() backend. Added automatic document YAML frontmatter format extraction via extract_yaml_formats() formats = "yaml" formats = "auto". Integrated computeGraph: document-level deliverable formats FileOutputs pipeline-level pipeline_config(default_formats = ...) seamlessly override package default c("pdf", "docx"). Expanded native support .qmd .Rmd documents (pattern = "\\.(qmd|Rmd|rmd)$"). Added engine = c("auto", "quarto", "rmarkdown") automatic shorthand format translation ("pdf" -> "pdf_document", "docx" -> "word_document", "html" -> "html_document", "gfm" -> "github_document"). Added anonymized eda_tables.qmd child_eda_chi_square.qmd inst/templates/ inst/rmarkdown/templates/eda-tables/ missingness diagnostics, stacked gtsummary baseline tables, association matrices, pairwise categorical comparisons. summarize_section_by_time() now defaults engine = "gtsummary", retaining engine = "arsenal" backwards-compatible fallback.

title: TempleCBE 0.3.403
text: Fixed critical issue SumNa(df, na_list = ...) failed detect sentinel values data frames due %% list dispatch. now traverses columns column--column, correctly counting standard NAs multi-code institutional sentinels (e.g. "999", "-99", "Unknown"). Fixed counting-process interval construction events occur scheduled longitudinal observation visits. Post-event filtering now occurs prior interval lead calculations, correctly setting tstop event time assigning event = 1 terminal intervals. Protected words() requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) provided native base R fallback Oxford comma text formatting, preventing runtime crashes minimal installs without knitr. Guarded fold_change log2_fold_change division zero negative values baseline group mean zero, safely returning NA_real_. calculate_fences() now gracefully returns NA_real_ bounds input vectors contain zero non-NA values, preventing unhandled quantile() exceptions. Standardized .outlier factor levels c(FALSE, TRUE) across data subsets. Aligned Python anonymizer R security policies: default confidential mapping file now stored user-scoped data directories (~/.TempleCBE/pi_mapping.json) outside git repository tree, automated repository root detection atomic file replacement. Synchronized @param n_chars documentation reflect default 16-character hexadecimal token length. Added data/, *.xlsx, *.csv, *.rds patterns root .gitignore safeguard accidental tracking clinical datasets. Updated scripts/clean_publish.sh default active working branch rather falling back unconditionally master.

what: Multivariable Cox Modeling, Kaplan-Meier, and Shared Diagnostics
title: TempleCBE 0.3.3141
text: New cbe_cox_multi() fits multivariable Cox proportional hazards model (via formula, outcome/features convenience pair), returning tidy coefficient table grouped variable explicit reference rows, glance fit summary, per-term global proportional hazards diagnostics, convergence status, formatted print() method. New cbe_cox_check() provides standalone, tidy cox.zph() diagnostics (per-term table, violation flags, automated text summary, including multivariate global test) coxph, cbe_cox, cbe_cox_multi object. cbe_cox_single() now uses cbe_cox_check() internally. New cbe_km_single() pairs univariable cbe_cox_single() fit matching stratified Kaplan-Meier curve (quartile-binned continuous predictors) without refitting Cox model twice, returning Cox object, survfit object, tidy KM table, hazard direction, combined summary table, formatted print() method. New cbe_cox_table() formats cbe_cox/cbe_cox_multi coefficient table presentation, adding log(HR) column optional sorting magnitude p-value significance-star annotation. New cbe_factor_reference() relevels factor’s reference level fitting, chosen level reported via message() recorded "cbe_reference_level" attribute. New cbe_theme_survival() gives single consistent ggplot2 look across Cox/KM visualizations; plot_cox_forest(), plot_cox_survival(), plot_cox_marginal() now use . plot_cox_forest() gains scale ("hr"/"log_hr"), color_by ("none"/"significance"), order_by ("none"/"magnitude"/"pvalue") arguments. New plot_cox_forest_multi() renders cbe_cox_multi() result forest plot per-variable facet blocks, sharing scale/color_by/order_by options plot_cox_forest(). plot_cox_survival() gains overlay_km = FALSE; TRUE, observed Kaplan-Meier step curves overlaid (dashed) Cox-predicted curves (solid), legend distinguishing two. plot_cox_marginal() gains scale ("prob"/"hr"/"log_hr") plot predicted event probability relative hazard (centered linear predictor), now draws confidence band Added ... argument passthrough cbe_cox_multi() cbe_cox_single(), supporting ties = "breslow", id = ID, cluster, advanced survival::coxph options. Added internal SAS Institute Example 85.7 validation datasets tumor_wide() (45 rodents, 19 variables) tumor_long() (102 counting-process intervals, 8 variables) time-dependent papilloma survival benchmarks. Added tidy_tmerge_cox() helper function construct counting-process start/stop intervals repeated longitudinal measurements event data frames baseline covariate integration. Added project-level pipeline orchestration script MakeComputeGraph.R (vignettes/ inst/scripts/) simulating Wolfson dependency graph architecture across four analytical stages. 01. eda_and_missingness.Rmd 02. nested_survival_cv.Rmd 03. compute_graph.Rmd 04. sas_survival.Rmd

what: Integrated Standard Biostatistical and Presentation Components from Wolfson

New reporting formatters: fmt_pct(), fmt_num(), fmt_sig(), fmt_p(), fmt_hr(), words(). New use_temple_brand() installs extension (jkylearmstrong-temple/quarto_temple_brand default) Quarto project, creating _quarto.yml needed, enables temple-html, temple-pdf (LaTeX title page), temple-typst, temple-revealjs formats. create_report(template_name = "temple") scaffolds report formats; install_brand = TRUE also installs extension. Plots use Temple palette. Diverging heatmaps (correlation_plot(), correlation_diff_heatmap(), pca_feature_loading_heatmap(), pca_loading_diff_heatmap()) run Night Owl-white-cherry instead blue-white-red; missmap() counts, plot_features_percent_miss(), plot_pca_bi()/pca_biplot() loadings, pca_percent_var_explained(), reference lines distribution_plot(), manhattan_plot(), volcano_plot() use Temple colors. colors change. palette follows Temple’s current brand (https://liberalarts.temple.edu/marcom/logos--brand), matching quarto_temple_brand: cherry, white, black (#000000); Clear Skies Book Nook; formal accents academic-gold, diamond-acres, founders-garden, night-owl; casual accents owls-eye, conwell-blue, upward-momentum, cherry-blossom. earlier names (taupe, icy-blue, lime, eggshell, ochre, geranium, dark-blue) gone. "main" palette cherry, Night Owl, Owl’s Eye, Founder’s Garden, Upward Momentum, Diamond Acres, black; "sequential" runs Book Nook cherry. Links bundled brand.yml standard blue (#0563c1) rather cherry, matching quarto_temple_brand. brand guide sets link color, red links read errors, especially print.
